script: My phone's volume shattered a quiet restaurant—everyone gasped, leaving me stunned.. The first time it happened, I was in a bustling diner, the kind with neon lights and the smell of fried onions. I had my phone glued to my ear, scrolling through reels while the TV blared a new episode. I didn't even notice the volume until the guy across the table leaned forward, eyes wide, and said, "Bro, can you hear that?" (I know, right?) I am like, "Yo, it's not that loud, dude. Just a normal volume." He snorts, "You're probably the only one who's hearing it." (Literally insane.) The whole table's eyes flicked to me, and I felt that instant heat of embarrassment. (I mean, who's going to be that oblivious?) Then, the next table—no, not another room, just a few seats over—had a woman with a toddler. She was scrolling, oblivious to the noise. Her kid started giggling, and the baby's mother glanced up, eyebrows popping. "Can you hear me?" she demanded, like a mom who just discovered a new level of parental control. I laughed, because it's like, "Do you seriously think I am the only one who can hear the world?" (Honestly, it's a meme.) People keep saying, "You're being a jerk. Shut up." But the real shock is the audacity of the reaction. (I mean, come on, your phone's not a bomb, it's just a device.) The stakes? You're either the quiet genius who's just keeping it low, or the loud guy who's a social hazard. I didn't want to be the hazard, so I lowered my phone. (But not enough for the kid's mother, apparently.) The whole scene played out like a silent movie in a noisy theater—everyone's watching, but nobody's listening. I was just trying to enjoy my reel, not to be the center of a public debate. And that's the tea: when your phone's loud enough for anyone nearby, it's not just a personal choice, it's a social signal. (And honestly, that's why we're all here, bestie.)
